title: 합계 10 규칙 단순화
problem: 합이 10이어도 위치 제약 때문에 거절되거나 가능한 조합이 남았는데 종료되는 문제가 보고됐다.
change: 앞선 2f371c8에서 같은 숫자 매칭을 없앤 뒤 이 커밋에서 직선·인접 조건과 무의미해진 셔플을 제거했다.
outcome: 어디에 있든 2~5개를 골라 합계 10이면 지워진다. 전후 비교는 직전 위치 제약 버전과 비교한다.
method: Historical git archive in isolated temp directory; current Vite runtime; fresh storage; seeded Math.random and controlled clock; finite animations finished. No historical source changes. Not a historical phone photograph or participant experiment.

before.commitMessage:
feat: sum-to-ten only, line of sight, fixed board

Removes same-number matching. A selection now clears only when two to five
tiles add up to exactly ten; repeated values inside a chain (1+1+8) are still
fine. Connection becomes a single rule — a straight line, horizontal, vertical
or diagonal, with no surviving tile in the way — replacing grid adjacency plus
the reading-order wrap that read as arbitrary on screen.

Three things had to change with it, each because simulation said so:

Boards are dealt as groups that already sum to ten rather than loose random
numbers. Every clear removes exactly ten, so the total's last digit never
changes; a random board is unclearable nine times in ten, and simulated runs
failed all 120 games with the board growing past 490 tiles.

The + action becomes a shuffle. Copying the survivors duplicated whatever the
player was stuck on — without same-number matching nothing broke the loop, and
leftovers climbed from 8 to 355 as more copies were spent. Shuffling keeps the
numbers and only moves them, so the board never grows.

Stage goals become star grades. A perfect clear turned out to depend on the
deal, not the player: on two of three sampled boards, 120 randomised
playthroughs never got below three tiles. Stars are scored on tiles left, with
targets set as a share of the board that tightens each stage.

The deal's group sizes work backwards from the obvious reading, so the comments
say so: many large groups make a board easier, since five values totalling ten
average two apiece and small numbers combine freely. Plain pairs spread the
values out and strand the rigid 8s and 9s.

The board is dealt at a fixed size and never grows, so it is laid out to fit
the screen — 5x8 at stage 1 up to 10x15 at stage 20, tiles sized to the space
available. Nothing scrolls, which leaves one-finger drag free for selection.

Greedy play now grades 2.42 stars at stage 1 falling to 0.92 at stage 20, every
stage passable. 70 unit tests, plus browser passes over the rules, the layout at
both board extremes, and all three modes.

after.commitMessage:
refactor: drop the position rule, reorganise into core/content/ui

Tiles may now be combined wherever they sit. A selection clears when two to
five surviving tiles add up to exactly ten, and nothing else is checked — no
adjacency, no straight line, no line of sight. That answers both reports:
1+1+1+7 totals ten and was only ever refused because the four tiles did not
share a line, and "nothing left to connect" fired while combinations were
still on the board.

The shuffle goes with it. Rearranging tiles cannot change a verdict that never
looks at position, so it had nothing left to do. A run now ends exactly when no
values on the board can make ten, which core/solver.ts answers from the nine
value counts rather than by walking the grid.

Two selection fixes this exposed: a tile that would push the running total past
ten now starts a fresh selection instead of piling onto an unclearable heap,
and tapping the board outside any tile abandons the selection.

Structure, since this will keep being edited:

  src/core/     rules engine — no DOM, fully tested
  src/content/  stage curve, star targets, chapters and lines
  src/ui/       screens, split into title / hud / overlay / story
  docs/         why it is built this way

Dependencies run one way, ui -> content -> core, so a skin change never reaches
the rules. The stylesheet is split to match, with the palette in tokens.css.

docs/DECISIONS.md records the findings that are counter-intuitive enough to be
undone by accident: random boards are mathematically unclearable because each
clear removes exactly ten and never changes the total's last digit; dealing
many large groups makes a board easier rather than harder; a perfect clear
depends on the deal, so three stars is a small number rather than an empty
board. Each entry carries the measurement behind it.

57 unit tests, plus browser passes over the rules, the layout at both board
extremes, all three modes and the chapter beat.
